findings.title: The prototype guard skips the final path segment, so '__proto__' can still be assigned as a leaf key
findings.recommendation: Run the banned-key check on every segment, including keys[keys.length - 1], and do it before the loop and before any read or write. Better still, reject '__proto__', 'constructor' and 'prototype' outright in any position. Also use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key) instead of obj[key] === undefined, and create intermediate containers with Object.create(null) or only write to own properties. The loop runs to keys.length - 1, so a path such as '/a/__proto__' with an object value reaches the final assignment (outside this diff) with key '__proto__'. That assignment calls the __proto__ setter and replaces the prototype of the target object with attacker-controlled data. For path '/__proto__' the loop does not run at all, so the document's own prototype can be swapped.

evaluations.reasoning: The hunk context shows the loop bound `i < keys.length - 1`, so the new `__proto__` guard never runs on the last path segment. A path like '/a/__proto__' or '/__proto__' therefore reaches the final assignment, which sits outside the diff, with `__proto__` as the key. For '/__proto__' the loop does not run at all. Assigning an object to `obj['__proto__']` invokes the prototype setter, so the guard is only partly effective, which fits CWE-1321 and INCOMPLETE-MITIGATION. The effect is limited to replacing the prototype of the target object or document. It does not reach Object.prototype. Medium severity is reasonable. The cited lines 6-10 cover the loop and the added check. The final-assignment behavior is inferred from the unchanged code rather than shown in the diff, but the loop bound is visible in the hunk context.

verifierOmissions.title: 'constructor' is not banned as an intermediate or leaf key, so the Object constructor can still be mutated
verifierOmissions.recommendation: Reject 'constructor' in any path position, or only traverse own properties using Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key). A path such as '/constructor/x' resolves obj['constructor'] to the Object function through the inherited lookup. The code then writes attacker-chosen properties onto it, which pollutes a global shared object. The guard only throws for 'prototype' when it directly follows 'constructor' (the `i > 0` condition), and it does nothing for inherited keys such as 'constructor' itself.
